title: Two send-offs after study
hookLine: an Upanishad's graduation speech, and a second text that says: go the very day it calls
carry: the ashramas honor both home and going forth
tomorrow: what does a student owe his teacher when the learning's done?

cards: Graduation speeches have a formula: follow your dreams, the world is yours, don't forget us.
The Taittiriya Upanishad has a graduation speech of its own, from a teacher to the student who is leaving, and it sounds nothing like that. It's a short list of plain instructions.
And another Upanishad, the Jabala, gives a very different send-off. Two voices, both inside the tradition. Let them talk.

teach.h: MOTHER, FATHER, TEACHER, GUEST: A GOD TO YOU.
teach.b: Having taught the Veda, the teacher instructs the student. Speak the truth. Practice dharma.
Don't neglect your study. Bring the teacher a gift, and don't cut off the line of your family. Then the lines still taught in many Hindu homes and schools: let your mother be a god to you.
Your father, a god to you. Your teacher, a god to you. Your guest, a god to you.

Give with faith, give with modesty. And if you're ever unsure what to do, act the way the thoughtful, gentle people near you who love dharma would act. Its best case: the world is where the learning gets used.
It lays out the ashramas, the four stages of a Hindu life: student, householder, forest dweller, and sannyasa, the life of one who has laid everything down.

teach.h: THE JABALA: GO THE DAY IT CALLS.
teach.b: Then it adds: or one may go forth straight from student life, or from the house, or from the forest. The very day the pull to let go arrives, that day, go.

Its best case: when the call comes, waiting can be its own way of saying no. Here's the teaching. Hinduism maps a life in stages, and honors both roads: the home, where dharma is lived with others, and going forth.
The Taittiriya doesn't call leaving wrong; the Jabala doesn't call the household small.

how: The Taittiriya's parting instruction (1.11), with its lines 'let your mother be a god to you, your father, your teacher, your guest', is widely taught in Indian homes and schools; the Jabala Upanishad is one of the texts later renunciant orders cite for leaving home.

a course that trains new priests for a temple

games.q: the Taittiriya's parting words. tap the pairs.
p: let each be a god to you
do as the gentle, wise people do

s: the Taittiriya's parting words tell the graduate that study is now over
'don't neglect your study' is right there on the list.
the Jabala allows going forth straight from student life
from student life, the house or the forest: the very day the pull to let go arrives.
the two texts condemn each other's path
the Jabala lays out the household stage too; the Taittiriya never calls leaving wrong.

games.q: you lean toward the householder's path. state the best case for the other side, in the Jabala's own terms.
o: the very day the pull to let go comes, go.
the world is evil, so get out of it early.
renunciants have no duties: the easy road.
games.why: the Jabala's case: when the call comes, go that day. it lays out the household stage too, so its point isn't that the world is evil; it's that the call can come at any stage.

practice: Join your palms at your chest and bow your head a little, the namaste offered to an elder. Then say softly the Taittiriya's four lines: mother, a god to me. Father, a god to me.
Teacher, a god to me. Guest, a god to me. At each one, picture a real face, here or gone.
If you don't pray, say it plainly: I honor my mother, my father, my teacher, the guest at my door.

wordCard.voice: The graduate's path: what comes after study. In the Taittiriya, a life in the world; in the Jabala, going forth the day it calls.

orig.note: Sanskrit: laying down, renunciation; the life of one who leaves home behind.

carryVoice: Your line: the ashramas honor both home and going forth. When unsure, look to the gentle and the wise. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11.1–4 (having taught the Veda, the teacher instructs the pupil: speak truth, practice dharma, do not neglect study; bring the teacher a gift, do not cut off the line of offspring; do not neglect welfare and prosperity; be one to whom mother, father, teacher and guest are as gods; give with faith, with modesty; in doubt about conduct, act as thoughtful, devoted, gentle brahmins who love dharma would act)

Jabala Upanishad 4 (having completed studenthood, become a householder; then a forest dweller; then go forth; or else go forth from studenthood, from the house or from the forest; the very day one becomes dispassionate, that very day go forth)
